results.title: Retention Isn't an HR Problem, It's a Leadership Problem | Melissa Hansel posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.content:
A few months later, they were fully staffed in key markets for the first time in 18 months.
What changed?
I showed the CEO her 360 results.
Every single person respected her.
Every single person also had an example of something that had fallen through the cracks.
A delayed decision.
An unanswered question.
A frustration they had learned to work around.
She finally saw it:
She wasn't helping by staying in everything.
She was slowing everything down.
And it was starting to affect how people felt about working there.
Here's the uncomfortable truth:
If something happened to you tomorrow, would your company know what to do?
Or would everything grind to a halt because you've trained the business to depend on you for everything?
Your team shouldn't need you for everything. [...] Finally I gave upper management an ultimatum: Fire him or I'm leaving, because when his long history of abuse is exposed, I don't want any liability for not trying to put an end to it.
They fired him instead.
Their fear of being exposed for coddling a psychopath was finally greater than their fear of an HR complaint since he "checked the boxes" for their diversity goals.
Two years later, while working with another client in the same industry... there was his name in one of the customer files we were reviewing. He had easily landed another job at a huge company.
The system, and former standards of excellence, are broken.
If you're company isn't making money hand over fist, maybe it is time to consider a different approach.
Link in the description. [...] Carla almost quit consulting.
And she wants you to know that because most people don't talk about this part.
The offers weren't landing.
Conversations felt completely one-sided.
The effort she was putting in simply wasn't showing up in her results.
She remembers thinking — maybe leaving corporate was the mistake.
Maybe this just isn't for me.
What pulled her through was one simple but powerful reframe:
Success in consulting isn't about never facing rejection.
It's about never letting rejection decide for you.
Most consultants quit right before things start to click.
They get ten no's and assume the offer is broken.
They get ghosted and assume they're not built for this.
They hit one slow month and start browsing job postings again.
But a no is just data.

results.title: Hansel & Gretel | Clive Hicks-Jenkins' Artlog:
results.content: In Simon Armitage’s extraordinary reworking of Hansel & Gretel, the children’s parents are not the malign mother and weak father of the Grimm Brothers’ original tale. Simon sets the story in an unnamed war-torn country, and the children are not abandoned but in an act of parental desperation, directed away from home and bombings. They’re migrant children. At the end of the story they return home to find their father broken, their home in ruins and their mother, dead and buried in a coffin made from their bomb-splintered beds. When making the illustrations for the book (Design for Today, 2019) I researched, made hundreds of studies and drew on memories that are always with me. [...] Why am I writing about all this now, so long after the event? Certainly not to persuade Kate Romano to change her mind about loaning the puppets. Over four years I’ve several times held out a hand of reconciliation in the hope of encouraging her to set aside resentments so we may together protect the legacy of what we made. I was and remain proud of my work on the stage production of Hansel & Gretel, and want to be able to share what was achieved in the exhibition. However everything I’ve written to Kate has gone unacknowledged and unanswered. There’s been not one e-mail reply to any of my attempts to lower the temperature of her antagonism. She is down a bunker in this matter, refusing to engage, and such behaviour in the world the way it is right now, is not a good look for anyone, let [...] which is not just something you can brush aside. There will be psychological scars. So the story is odd and downright nasty and has too often been glossed in endless re-tellings. It was just too good a chance to miss.”
